name: Making UIs Feel Alive w/ Shaders
tagline: Designer essay on replacing hand-built animated gradients with Framer Shaders
description: A practitioner essay arguing that most polished UIs look clean but read as flat, and that motion in the background layer is what gives a page texture and weight. The author walks through the old cost of animated gradients (mesh nodes, slideshow-grade prototypes, hours per hero) and then through Framer's built-in Shaders feature: animated gradients, image effects, and particles driven by sliders, with no code or libraries. It closes with five restraint rules, starting with 'do not make it the whole background'. Aimed at product and web designers who want a hero or card layer that feels bespoke without shipping a WebGL bundle by hand.
agent_guidance: Treat this as taste guidance, not a dependency: it tells you when an animated gradient or particle layer earns its place (hero backdrop at low opacity, card border, one section) and when it becomes noise. Relevant only if the target is a Framer site, because the Shaders feature is native to Framer and has no npm equivalent — for a React or Next build you would reach for a shader/gradient library instead and carry over only the restraint rules. Do not cite it as a spec; there are no tokens, params, or code in it.
why_it_matters: It names the specific failure mode of agent- and template-generated UI — technically clean, emotionally dead — and gives a concrete, cheap remedy with usage limits attached.

name: AI-Native Designer
tagline: Defines AI-native vs AI-augmented design work and the five workflow shifts between them
description: An essay that draws a hard line between an AI-augmented designer (same workflow, faster tools) and an AI-native one (a workflow that would be impossible without an agent in the loop). Its test is blunt: if you could still do your job in 2023 with the AI features off, you are augmented. The five named shifts include designing in code rather than mockups — the Figma file becomes a thinking surface and the deliverable is a working Next.js page on a real URL — and writing the design system as a prompt: a CLAUDE.md, a design.md, and a tailwind.config.ts, versioned in git and read by Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Lovable, v0, and Figma. For designers deciding how much of their process to rebuild.
agent_guidance: Use this to justify and shape the three-file design-system layout a user asks you to set up — CLAUDE.md for rules, design.md for the visual system, tailwind.config.ts for the tokens — rather than pushing them toward a Figma library you cannot read. It is a position piece, so mine it for structure, not for token values; it specifies no scales, no palette, no component contracts. Pair it with a real token source (a shadcn registry or a published design system) before you generate anything.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest short statement of the thesis this whole index rests on: the design system that matters is the one an agent can read from the repo.

name: Midjourney
tagline: Subscription text-to-image and image-to-video generation, via web app or Discord
description: Midjourney is a hosted generative image service known for the strongest default aesthetic in the category — it biases hard toward a rendered, art-directed look rather than literal prompt transcription. The web app at midjourney.com is now the primary interface (Discord still works) and carries the full feature set: an editor, style references (--sref), character references, upscaling, variations, and an Explore feed of public generations. It also ships an image-to-video model that animates a still into short clips, plus the Niji line for anime and illustration. There is no free tier; every paid plan includes a commercial-use license.
pricing_detail: Basic $10/mo, Standard $30/mo, Pro $60/mo, Mega $120/mo; roughly 20% off with annual billing ($8 / $24 / $48 / $96 per month). Fast GPU hours per month: 3.3 / 15 / 30 / 60. Standard and above add unlimited Relax generation; Pro and above add Stealth mode. No free tier since March 2023.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when a project needs hero art, texture plates, or brand imagery with a strong point of view, and accept that you cannot automate it — there is no public API and the site hard-403s scripted requests, so hand the user a prompt to run themselves rather than promising generated assets in your pipeline. It is the wrong tool for UI mockups, icon sets, or anything needing legible text or exact dimensions; use it for atmosphere and pair it with a real icon set and a real typeface. Budget GPU minutes: one still is about a minute, an HD video batch about 26.
why_it_matters: Still the aesthetic benchmark other image models are measured against, which makes it the default source for the one or two hero images a landing page actually lives or dies on.
notable_for: commercial license on all paid tiers

name: Claude Code for Designers
tagline: Step-by-step guide to going from wireframe to working UI with Claude Code, no coding
description: A designer-facing walkthrough of Claude Code that reframes the terminal as just a text box for instructions. It covers the five-minute setup, a copy-paste prompt skeleton for describing a screen (named elements, style, background, font), and then the iteration loop: look at the output, isolate one thing that is wrong, and say only that. The argument is that a designer's eye for what is off is the actual skill the workflow needs, which puts designers ahead of developers on this tool rather than behind. For designers who have never opened a terminal and want a real URL by the end of an afternoon.
agent_guidance: This is a resource to hand a non-technical user, not one to consult yourself — point them at it when they keep giving you vague briefs, because its prompt skeleton forces the element-by-element specificity that makes your first output usable. Its stated workflow starts from nothing (no framework, no stack decision), so if the user is already in a repo, ignore that framing and honor the existing stack. Note it prescribes no design system, so a build following it verbatim will drift unless you pin tokens first.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest on-ramp piece for the designer half of the audience, and it sets the expectation that the deliverable is a running page rather than a mockup.

name: 48 Laws of Web Design
tagline: 48 blunt landing-page rules for startups, with thresholds you can actually check
description: A numbered checklist of startup web-design rules written by a working designer, stated as constraints rather than principles: headline under 15 words, one CTA per viewport, social proof above the fold, at most two fonts per page, 5-6 nav items maximum, one question answered per section, exactly three steps in the how-it-works block, logo around 40px. It is opinionated about tradeoffs too — pricing must be visible, mobile is the primary view for roughly 62% of traffic, load time can outweigh visual polish, product screenshots outrank illustrations, testimonials with faces outrank text-only, and mixed outlined-and-filled icon styles read as amateur. Useful as a pre-launch pass over a marketing site.
agent_guidance: Run this as a review pass after you generate a marketing page, not as a generator — most of its rules are countable (word count, CTA count, font count, nav items, steps) so you can self-check a page against them mechanically before handing it back. Treat the aesthetic claims (dark backgrounds read premium, gradients are back) as dated-on-arrival taste, and ignore its silence on accessibility: several rules, notably the contrast-at-all-costs CTA advice, need a real contrast check on top. Do not cite the 62% mobile figure as sourced.
why_it_matters: Landing-page advice usually arrives as vibes; this one arrives as thresholds, which is the form an agent can actually enforce.

name: Psychology of a $1M Landing Page
tagline: Landing-page structure explained through named cognitive effects and where each applies
description: A breakdown of high-converting landing pages organized by the cognitive principle behind each structural choice. It covers the serial position effect (strongest claim in the hero, strongest proof or urgency right before the final CTA, details in the forgettable middle), the Von Restorff effect (the CTA must break the visual pattern — the Stripe example of a contrasting button on a blue gradient), cognitive load theory (working memory holds about four items, so 3-4 bullets per section and icon grids instead of text lists), and social proof cascading, where placement matters more than testimonial quality. For anyone deciding section order rather than section styling.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when you are ordering the sections of a marketing page, which is the decision templates make for you and usually make badly — it tells you what belongs first, what belongs last, and that the middle can absorb detail. It pairs with the 48-laws checklist: this one sets sequence and density, that one sets the per-element thresholds. The conversion percentages in it are unsourced rhetoric, so use the structural rules and drop the numbers.
why_it_matters: It converts landing-page folklore into a small set of named effects, which makes the reasoning transferable to layouts the article never mentions.
notable_for: serial position effect for section order
